waec-government-theory-0344.explanation: (a) (i) Religious and Judicial control: The village priest/ diviner wielded a great deal of religious and judicial powers. (ii) Leadership: Succession to leadership and to prominence was based on personal achievements (iii) Bonds and Unity: Deities are of political significance in providing bonds and unity. (iv) Market Square: It served as the village chambers. (v) Socio-political group: The women (Umuada) composed of the first daughter of each family, constituted a socio-political group. (vi) Banishment: Banishment from the village and escort of such people into the evil forest was the maximum judicial punishment. (vii) New yam festival: This was religiously marked, honoured and celebrated annually. (viii) Decentralized administration: Different authorities, groups and institutions took part in the administration. (b) (I) The executive: the affairs of the village were discussed and executed from time to time by family heads (council of elders) who formed the executive arm (ii) The legislature: The people in this society made laws themselves, and even the age-grades could enact a law that would be accepted by the elders. (iii) The judiciary: The family heads championed the settlement of disputes between families, Serious cases were referred to the council of elders presided over by the Okpara and penalties were meted out to those who committed serious offenses like murder, stealing, etc. (iv) The Ozo titleholders: Some wealthy and influential men took this title which was very expensive. This title made the holder recognized in the society and could then preside over meetings on issues affecting the community with elders. (v) Consensus: Critical issues before the authorities at the village assembly were reached by consensus. (vi) Council of elders: There was the existence of a council of elders (Ama-ala) presided over by the eldest son in the village. (vii) Value of individual personality: In a democracy, the belief in the value of individual personality is restored. It implies the need to respect the other man, to listen to his arguments and take into account his point of view.

waec-government-theory-0345.explanation: Democracy is widely regarded as a popular and effective system of governance due to several key factors that ensure broad participation, accountability and adherence to the rule of law. Here’s how each factor contributes to the popularity and effectiveness of democratic systems: 1. A System of Electing and Replacing Government: Democracy provides a structured process for electing government officials and allows for their replacement through regular elections. This system ensures that leaders are chosen by the people and can be held accountable through periodic voting. It prevents the entrenchment of power and supports government responsiveness to the electorate's needs and preferences. 2. Popular Participation by Citizens in Government: In a democracy, citizens have the right and opportunity to participate in governance through voting, running for office and engaging in public discourse. This participation empowers individuals to influence government policies and decisions. 3. Practice of Rule of Law: The rule of law ensures that all individuals, including government officials, are subject to the law and that laws are applied consistently and fairly. This principle prevents arbitrary governance and protects the rights and freedoms of individuals. 4. Multi-Party System: A multi-party system allows for a diversity of political parties and viewpoints, provides voters with a range of choices and promotes political competition. This diversity encourages more representative and inclusive governance as different perspectives and interests are considered in policy-making. 5. Majority Rule: Democracy operates on the principle of majority rule, where decisions are made based on the preferences of the majority of voters. This principle ensures that the decisions reflect the will of the majority while still respecting minority rights. It promotes effective governance and legitimacy as policies and leaders are chosen by the majority. 6. Supremacy of the Constitution: The supremacy of the Constitution means that it is the highest legal authority and all laws and government actions must comply with it. This principle provides a stable legal framework, protects individual rights and ensures that government powers are exercised within constitutional limits. 7. Separation of Powers/Checks and Balances: The separation of powers divides government responsibilities among different branches (executive, legislative, and judicial) to prevent any single branch from becoming too powerful. Checks and balances allow each branch to oversee and limit the actions of the others to ensure accountability and protect against abuses of power. 8. Free, Fair, and Periodic Elections: Democratic systems are characterised by free and fair elections that are held regularly. Free elections allow citizens to choose their leaders without coercion, while fair elections ensure that the process is transparent and unbiased. Periodic elections provide opportunities for political renewal and accountability.

waec-government-theory-0346.explanation: Several factors limit the power of government and ensure that it operates within established boundaries and respects democratic principles. Some of these factors are: 1. Constitutional Limitation: The constitution serves as the supreme legal document that outlines the structure of government, delineates the powers and responsibilities of various branches, and establishes the rights of citizens. Constitutional limitations define what each branch of government can and cannot do, providing a framework for legal and institutional constraints on government power. 2. Rule of Law Guides Against Arbitrary Rule: The rule of law ensures that all actions by the government are based on established laws rather than arbitrary decisions. It mandates that laws apply equally to everyone, including those in positions of power. This principle prevents government officials from acting beyond their legal authority and ensures accountability. 3. Customs and Traditions of the People: The customs and traditions of a society can limit government power by influencing the values and norms that guide governance. Traditional practices and societal expectations can shape legal and political systems and provide informal checks on government actions. 4. International Conventions and Agreements: Governments are often bound by international conventions and agreements that limit their actions and set standards for behaviour. These agreements, such as human rights treaties and trade agreements, create external constraints on government policies and actions and promote adherence to international norms and standards. 5. Regulatory Enforcement Mechanisms: Regulatory agencies and enforcement mechanisms help ensure that government policies and laws are implemented fairly and consistently. These bodies monitor compliance, investigate violations and impose penalties, thereby limiting the potential for government overreach and ensuring adherence to established rules and standards. 6. A Vibrant Opposition: An active and vocal opposition provides a critical check on government power by challenging policies, questioning decisions, and offering alternative viewpoints. This opposition plays a role in ensuring that government actions are subject to scrutiny and debate. 7. Party Discipline/Party Caucus: Within political parties, discipline and caucus mechanisms help manage internal disagreements and maintain unity. While this can sometimes consolidate power, it can also limit the extent to which party leaders can act unilaterally by ensuring that decisions are made collectively and in line with party policies and values. 8. Judicial Independence/Judicial Review: Judicial independence allows courts to make decisions based on the law without influence from the executive or legislative branches. Judicial review empowers the judiciary to examine and potentially overturn government actions that are unconstitutional or exceed legal authority. All of these provide a crucial check on governmental power. 9. Vibrant/Independent Media: A free and independent media plays a key role in monitoring and exposing government actions. By reporting on government activities, investigating corruption and providing a platform for public discourse, the media holds the government accountable and informs the public about governmental decisions and policies. 10. Ethnic/Tribal/Religious Considerations: Considerations related to ethnicity, tribe and religion can influence governmental decision-making and limit the scope of government actions. In diverse societies, governments must navigate and respect these considerations to maintain social harmony and avoid discrimination, which can act as a constraint on how policies are formulated and implemented.

waec-government-theory-0347.explanation: The independence of the judiciary is a fundamental principle in democratic governance as it ensures that courts can operate impartially and without undue influence. The following are reasons the judiciary needs to be independent: 1. For the Purpose of Fair Judgements: An independent judiciary ensures that judges can make decisions based on the law and facts of each case, without external pressures or biases. This impartiality is essential for delivering fair and just outcomes and maintaining trust in the legal system. 2. Prevent Arbitrary Acts/Rule: Independence helps prevent the executive or legislature from exerting undue influence on judicial decisions. Without this independence, there is a risk that legal rulings could be swayed by political motives or personal interests, leading to arbitrary and unjust rulings. 3. Prevent Autocracy/Dictatorship: An independent judiciary serves as a check on the power of the executive and legislative branches, reducing the risk of autocratic or dictatorial rule. By ensuring that the judiciary can act independently, it helps maintain a balance of power and prevents any single branch of government from becoming too dominant. 4. Protection of Individual/Group Rights: Judicial independence is crucial for safeguarding individual and group rights. Courts must be able to protect rights and freedoms without fear of retaliation or coercion from other branches of government. This protection is essential for upholding civil liberties and ensuring justice for all citizens. 5. For the Maintenance of the Rule of Law: The rule of law requires that laws be applied consistently and fairly. An independent judiciary ensures that legal principles are upheld and that all individuals are subject to the same legal standards, regardless of their position or influence. 6. To Ensure Checks and Balances in Constitutional Government: Judicial independence supports the system of checks and balances by enabling the judiciary to review and challenge actions by the executive and legislative branches. This oversight helps maintain constitutional limits on power and ensures that government actions comply with the law. 7. To Ensure Public Confidence in Government/Judiciary: When the judiciary operates independently, it enhances public confidence in both the judicial system and the broader government. Trust in the fairness and impartiality of the courts is essential for maintaining legitimacy and ensuring that legal decisions are respected and accepted. 8. To Ensure Free and Fair Elections: An independent judiciary plays a critical role in overseeing and adjudicating electoral disputes and ensures that elections are conducted fairly and that any issues are resolved impartially. This independence helps protect the integrity of the electoral process and the democratic system. 9. To Insulate the Judiciary from Partisan Politics: Independence protects the judiciary from being influenced by political considerations and partisan interests. By keeping judges free from political pressures, the judicial system can focus on interpreting and applying the law impartially, rather than being swayed by political agendas. 10. To Ensure Judicial Professional Integrity: Independence supports judicial professional integrity by allowing judges to make decisions based solely on legal principles and evidence. This freedom from external influences helps maintain high standards of professionalism and ethical conduct within the judiciary.

waec-government-theory-0348.explanation: Public opinion plays a crucial role in the democratic process through the following ways: 1. It Allows for Freedom of Expression: Public opinion reflects the freedom of individuals to express their views, beliefs and concerns. In a democratic society, this freedom is fundamental as it ensures that diverse perspectives are heard and considered. Freedom of expression fosters open dialogue and helps to identify and address issues within the society. 2. It Allows for Citizens' Participation in Government Processes: Public opinion is a measure of citizen engagement in the democratic process. By participating in public debates, elections and other civic activities, citizens contribute to shaping government policies and decisions. This participation ensures that the government reflects the will and needs of the people. 3. Gives Feedback to Government in Power: Public opinion provides valuable feedback to those in power about their policies and actions. Governments can gauge public satisfaction or dissatisfaction through opinion polls, surveys and public forums. This feedback helps leaders adjust their policies to better align with the desires and concerns of the populace. 4. Influences Public Policy Formulation and Implementation: Policymakers often consider public opinion when formulating and implementing policies. Widespread support or opposition to certain issues can drive legislators to adopt or modify policies. Public opinion thus plays a key role in ensuring that policies are responsive to the needs and values of the society. 5. **Device for Effective Control of the Government:** Public opinion acts as a mechanism for controlling government actions by holding officials accountable for their performance. If public opinion is strongly negative, it can lead to political pressure, protests, or changes in leadership. This control helps prevent abuses of power and ensures that the government remains responsive to the public. 6. Ensures Accountability and Transparency in Government: A government that is aware of and responsive to public opinion is more likely to be accountable and transparent. Public scrutiny and criticism help to uncover and address issues of corruption, inefficiency, or unethical behavior, promoting a more open and accountable government. 7. It Gives Direction to Government Actions/Decisions: Public opinion provides direction for government actions and decisions by highlighting the priorities and concerns of the citizens. When governments understand what issues are most important to the public, they can focus their efforts and resources on addressing those areas. 8. It Assists in the Promotion of the Rights and Freedoms of the Citizens: Public opinion can advocate for the protection and expansion of individual rights and freedoms. By voicing support for civil rights issues, social justice, and equitable treatment, public opinion can drive reforms and policies that enhance the rights and freedoms of citizens. 9. Serves as an Agent of Social Change: Public opinion is a powerful force for social change. When large segments of the population advocate for change, whether on issues like gender equality, environmental protection, or human rights, it can lead to significant shifts in policies, laws, and societal norms. 10. It Guides the Undecided Voters: Public opinion helps guide undecided voters by providing insights into the prevailing sentiments and stances on various issues. During elections, the prevailing public opinion can influence the decisions of undecided voters, helping them make informed choices based on the general consensus or direction of the electorate.

waec-government-theory-0349.explanation: To ensure that local governments effectively fulfil their mandate and manage resources efficiently, various control mechanisms can be employed. Here are some of them: 1. Executive/Administrative Control: The executive branch or administrative authorities at higher levels of government can exercise control over local governments through oversight and directive powers. This involves setting guidelines, monitoring the implementation of policies and ensuring compliance with national standards. 2. Threats of Dissolution: Higher levels of government, such as state or national authorities, can use the threat of dissolution to enforce accountability. If a local government fails to perform its duties or engages in corruption, the central authority might threaten to dissolve the local government and appoint an administrator or take over its functions. 3. Scrutiny of Procurement Processes: To prevent corruption and ensure proper use of resources, the procurement processes of local governments can be scrutinized. This involves reviewing and auditing how contracts are awarded and ensuring that procurement procedures comply with legal and ethical standards. Scrutiny helps ensure transparency and accountability in how local governments acquire goods and services. 4. Performance Appraisal Contract: Performance appraisal contracts are agreements that set specific performance targets and standards for local government officials. These contracts include clear metrics for evaluating success and effectiveness. By linking performance to these contracts, local governments can be held accountable for meeting their objectives and providing quality services. 5. Legislative/Parliamentary Control: Legislative or parliamentary bodies at the state or national level have the authority to oversee and review the actions of local governments. This control includes passing laws that affect local governance, reviewing budgets and expenditures, and holding hearings to assess performance. Legislative control ensures that local governments operate within legal frameworks and adhere to policy directives. 6. Control by the Press: The media plays a critical role in monitoring and reporting on the activities of local governments. Through investigative journalism and regular reporting, the press can highlight issues of corruption, mismanagement, and inefficiency. Public exposure through the media can prompt corrective actions and enhance accountability. 7. Periodic Audit: Regular audits conducted by independent agencies or internal audit departments assess the financial and operational activities of local governments. Audits help identify discrepancies, inefficiencies, and areas of concern, providing recommendations for improvement. Periodic auditing ensures that local governments adhere to financial regulations and manage resources effectively. 8. Public Opinion: Local governments are accountable to the public, and their actions can be influenced by public opinion. Community feedback, petitions, and public meetings allow citizens to express their views and concerns. When local governments are aware of and responsive to public opinion, they are more likely to align their activities with the needs and expectations of their constituents. 9. Sanctioning Unsatisfactory Performance: Mechanisms for sanctioning unsatisfactory performance include disciplinary actions, removal from office, or other penalties for local government officials who fail to meet their responsibilities. These sanctions serve as a deterrent against poor performance and ensure that local governments adhere to their mandates. 10. Withholding/Reducing Grants: Higher levels of government can control local governments by withholding or reducing financial grants and allocations. Since local governments often depend on these funds for their operations and projects, the threat or actual reduction of grants can motivate them to improve their performance and compliance with regulations.

waec-government-theory-0350.explanation: (a) i. The Royalty (Afin) ii. The Kingmakers (Oyomesi) iii. Cult (Ogoni) iv. The Osi Efa v. The Oni Efa vi. The Otun Efa vii. Army (Are Onakakanfo) (b) In the Yoruba precolonial system, checks and balances were integral to governance because it ensured accountability and prevented the abuse of power. The following were some of the checks and balances that were present in the Yoruba precolonial system: 1. Oath of Office: Chiefs and rulers in Yoruba society were required to take oaths of office, pledging their loyalty and commitment to their duties and the welfare of their subjects. These oaths were serious and were believed to invoke spiritual or divine sanctions. The oath served as a moral and legal obligation, helping to ensure that chiefs acted in accordance with the established norms and values and therefore minimised the risk of corruption and misuse of power. 2. The Traditional Three Arms of Government (Oba/Oyomesi/Ogboni) Checked One Another: The Oba: The traditional king or ruler. (executive) The Oyomesi: A council of high chiefs who acted as advisors and were involved in major decisions, including the selection and dethronement of the Oba. (legislature) The Ogboni: A powerful council with judicial and advisory functions, often tasked with enforcing traditional laws and maintaining social order. (judiciary) These three arms of government had distinct roles but also checked each other. For example, the Oyomesi and Ogboni could challenge or question the actions of the Oba, and their combined authority ensured that no single body could unilaterally dominate the governance process. 3. Impeachment/Dethronement: Chiefs and rulers could be impeached or dethroned if they were deemed to have failed in their duties or abused their power. The process for removing a ruler involved serious consultations and, in some cases, a formal decision by the Oyomesi or Ogboni. This served as a powerful check on the ruler’s power, ensuring that leaders remained accountable to the people and traditional institutions. When the Oyomesi decides that the Oba is no longer fit to rule, he will be sentenced to death by suicide. 4. The Oracle (Ifa) Made Predictions and Advised on Precautionary Measures: The Oracle, particularly Ifa, played a significant role in Yoruba governance. It was used for divination to provide guidance on important decisions and to predict potential outcomes. The advice given by the Oracle was highly respected and often influenced major decisions and policies. This spiritual oversight provided an additional layer of accountability, as leaders were expected to heed the Oracle’s warnings and recommendations to avoid missteps and calamities. 5. An Occult Calabash (Igba-Iwa); To Checkmate Abuse of Power: The Igba-Iwa was a traditional instrument used to monitor and check abuses of power. It was believed to hold spiritual significance and had the power to reveal misconduct or ethical breaches. The presence of such a symbolic object served as a deterrent against corruption and misuse of authority, as leaders knew that their actions could be exposed and judged by these spiritual means.

waec-government-theory-0351.explanation: The Independence Constitution of 1960, which marked Nigeria’s transition to self-government from British colonial rule, had several weaknesses that reflected the lingering influence of colonialism and some gaps in its framework. Here are some of them: 1. Vestiges of Colonialism as the Queen Remained the Constitutional Head of State: Under the 1960 Constitution, the Queen of England was retained as the constitutional Head of State, represented by a Governor-General in Nigeria. This arrangement maintained a symbolic link to colonial rule and undermined Nigeria's full sovereignty and the sense of complete independence from British authority. 2. The Judicial Committee of the British House of Lords in London Was Still the Highest Court of Appeal: The constitution retained the Judicial Committee of the British House of Lords as the highest court of appeal for Nigerian legal matters. This meant that Nigerian legal decisions could be appealed to a British institution, which limited Nigeria’s judicial independence and reinforced colonial influence in the legal system. 3. The Constitution Did Not State Whether or Not Appointments into Public Offices Were to Be Based on Federal Character: The 1960 Constitution did not address the principle of federal character, which refers to the fair distribution of public offices and positions among Nigeria's various ethnic groups. This omission left room for potential bias and favoritism in appointments, which exacerbated ethnic tensions and inequality in the distribution of power and resources. 4. The Constitutional Making Process Was Not Entirely Undertaken by Nigerians: The process of drafting and adopting the 1960 Constitution involved significant input from British officials and was not entirely led by Nigerians. This lack of complete Nigerian involvement in the constitutional process meant that the document might not fully reflect the aspirations and needs of the Nigerian people, as it was influenced by colonial perspectives and interests. 5. The Constitution Failed to Specify the Number of Ministers to Be Appointed: The 1960 Constitution did not provide a specific number of ministers to be appointed at the federal level. This lack of detail led to ambiguity and potential inconsistency in the composition of the executive branch, which could affect the efficiency and effectiveness of governance. 6. The Constitution Did Not State That Its Provisions Were Supreme: The 1960 Constitution did not explicitly declare its provisions as supreme over other laws. This lack of a clear supremacy clause meant that the Constitution could potentially be overridden or ignored by other legislative or executive actions. This undermines its authority and stability as the foundational legal document of the country.

waec-government-theory-0352.explanation: Nigeria has faced several challenges in its international interactions. Here are five notable problems: 1. Diplomatic Tensions and Conflicts: Nigeria has experienced diplomatic tensions with various countries over issues such as border disputes and regional influence. For example, disputes with neighbouring countries over the Bakassi Peninsula and the Niger Delta have strained relations. These conflicts have sometimes led to diplomatic and economic repercussions. 2. Loss of Citizens Through Peacekeeping Operations: Nigeria has contributed troops to various peacekeeping missions under the United Nations and the African Union. The loss of Nigerian soldiers in these operations has had humanitarian and political repercussions and has impacted Nigeria's national pride and its international standing. 3. The influx of Refugees and Its Impact on the Economy: Conflicts and instability in neighbouring countries have led to a significant influx of refugees into Nigeria. This has placed a strain on Nigeria’s resources, infrastructure and public services which has led to economic challenges and social tensions. 4. Economic Dependencies and Trade Imbalances: Nigeria's reliance on oil exports has made its economy vulnerable to fluctuations in global oil prices. This dependency has sometimes led to trade imbalances and economic instability and has affected Nigeria's position in international trade and its relationships with other nations. 5. Corruption and Governance Issues: Corruption within Nigeria's government and institutions has impacted its international standing. Issues such as mismanagement of funds, lack of transparency and poor governance have led to strained relationships with foreign partners and challenges in securing international aid and investment. Others include: 6. Human Rights and Security Concerns: Nigeria has faced criticism from the international community over human rights abuses and security issues. The ongoing conflict with Boko Haram and other insurgent groups has drawn attention to the country's security situation and its handling of human rights concerns, affecting its global image and relations. 7. Immigration and Diaspora Issues: Nigeria has faced challenges related to its diaspora and immigration policies. Issues such as the treatment of Nigerian migrants abroad and the management of remittances have sometimes caused friction between Nigeria and other countries. Additionally, the treatment of Nigerian expatriates and students has occasionally strained diplomatic relations. 8. Increase in Crime Rates by Some Foreign Nationals: The presence of foreign nationals in Nigeria has sometimes been linked to increased crime rates, including trafficking and smuggling. This can lead to tensions between local communities and foreign residents and complicate Nigeria’s international relations. 9. Smuggling Across Nigerian Borders: Nigeria faces challenges with smuggling, particularly of goods like arms and drugs, across its porous borders. This illegal activity undermines national security, affects legitimate trade and creates diplomatic issues with neighbouring countries. 10. Ideological Differences Among Nations: Nigeria’s foreign policy can be complicated by ideological differences with other nations. These differences can affect bilateral relations and Nigeria’s role in international organisations and impact its ability to form effective partnerships and alliances. 11. Clear Definition of National Interest: Ambiguities in Nigeria’s national interests can sometimes lead to inconsistent foreign policy decisions and difficulties in international negotiations. Clear and consistent definitions of national interests are crucial for effective international engagement. 12. Regional Insecurity: Insecurity in the West African region, including conflicts and terrorist activities, can spill over into Nigeria. This regional instability affects Nigeria’s security and its interactions with neighboring countries, complicating efforts for

waec-government-theory-0353.explanation: While colonial rule in West Africa had many negative impacts, it also brought some positive changes. Here are five positive impacts of British and French colonial administration in West Africa: 1. Infrastructure Development: Colonial administrations invested in building infrastructure such as roads, railways, ports and telecommunication networks. This infrastructure facilitated transportation and communication, which are essential for economic development and modernization. 2. Education: The colonial powers established schools and introduced Western-style education. This led to increased literacy rates and provided educational opportunities that were previously unavailable. Many of the leaders of post-independence Africa were products of these colonial education systems. 3. Healthcare Improvements: Colonial governments introduced modern healthcare systems, including hospitals, clinics and public health campaigns. This helped to combat diseases, reduce mortality rates and improve overall public health standards. 4. Legal and Administrative Systems: The introduction of formal legal and administrative systems helped to establish order and a structured governance framework. These systems often included codified laws, judiciary systems and bureaucratic institutions that many countries retained and adapted after independence. 5. Economic Integration and Development: Colonial rule integrated West African economies into the global economic system. This integration brought new economic activities, such as cash crop farming and mining, which helped to develop the economies of the region. Additionally, the colonial emphasis on developing export economies laid the groundwork for modern economic systems. Others include: 6. Introduction of Modern Technology and Techniques: Colonial administrations introduced modern agricultural techniques, machinery and other technologies. These advancements helped improve agricultural productivity and introduced new crops and farming methods. 7. Urbanisation: The colonial period saw the growth of urban centers and cities, which became hubs of economic activity, trade and administration. These urban centers often provided more opportunities for education, employment and social services. 8. Standardisation of Language: The introduction of English and French as official languages helped create a unifying medium of communication across diverse ethnic groups. This standardisation facilitated better communication within colonies and with the outside world. 9. Economic Diversification: The colonial powers encouraged the development of various economic sectors such as mining, agriculture and trade. This diversification helped lay the foundation for more complex economic systems in the post-colonial period. 10. Cultural Exchange: Colonial rule brought about cultural exchanges, which led to the introduction of new ideas, religions and cultural practices. This exchange enriched the cultural landscape of West Africa, despite also leading to cultural assimilation and loss of indigenous practices.

waec-government-theory-0354.explanation: When the military took over the administration of Nigeria, democracy was stalled in several ways. Here are five key ways in which this happened: 1. Suspension of the Constitution: Each military regime typically suspended the existing constitution, which is the foundational legal document that outlines the democratic framework of the country. This suspension effectively halted democratic governance and replaced it with military rule. 2. Dissolution of Democratic Institutions: Military regimes often dissolved democratic institutions such as the National Assembly (parliament), state assemblies and local government councils. This dissolution removed the legislative and representative bodies that are essential for a functioning democracy. 3. Suppression of Political Parties and Activities: Political parties were frequently banned or heavily restricted under military rule. This suppression curtailed political pluralism and competition, which are important elements of democracy. Political activities, including rallies, campaigns and elections, were often prohibited. 4. Centralisation of Power: Military rulers centralised power in the executive branch, often concentrating authority in the hands of a single military leader or a small group of military officers. This concentration of power undermined the principle of checks and balances that is fundamental to democratic governance. 5. Human Rights Violations and Lack of Freedoms: Military regimes often ruled with an iron fist. Thid led to widespread human rights abuses, including arbitrary arrests, detentions without trial, torture and extrajudicial killings. Freedoms of speech, press, assembly and association were severely curtailed and this stifled the democratic expression of dissent and opposition. Others include 6. A culture of silence was instituted. 7. Tendency to hold on to power. 8. The rule of law was disregarded.

waec-government-theory-0365.explanation: The government, as an agent of the state, performs several functions. These include: - Law-making: The government formulates and implements laws to guide the conduct of citizens. - Maintenance of Law and Order: The government ensures peace and security through law enforcement agencies. - Provision of Public Goods and Services: The government provides essential services such as education, healthcare, and infrastructure. - Protection of Rights and Liberties: The government protects the fundamental rights and freedoms of its citizens. - Economic Management: The government manages the economy through fiscal and monetary policies to ensure economic stability and growth.

waec-government-theory-0366.explanation: Several factors can hamper the effective operation of the justice delivery system. These include: - Corruption: This undermines the integrity of the justice system. - Inadequate Funding: Lack of sufficient funds can lead to delays and inefficiencies. - Poor Infrastructure: Inadequate facilities can hinder the administration of justice. - Inadequate Manpower: A shortage of trained personnel can affect the delivery of justice. - Political Interference: This can compromise the independence of the judiciary.

waec-government-theory-0367.explanation: Several factors have contributed to the weakening of government institutions in many West African States. These include: - Corruption: This undermines the effectiveness and credibility of government institutions. - Political Instability: Frequent changes in government can disrupt the functioning of institutions. - Poor Governance: Lack of transparency and accountability can weaken institutions. - Inadequate Funding: Lack of resources can hinder the performance of institutions. - Weak Rule of Law: This can undermine the authority and effectiveness of institutions.

waec-government-theory-0368.explanation: Political socialization assists in the democratic process of a state in several ways. These include: - Formation of Political Opinions: Through political socialization, individuals develop their political beliefs and opinions. - Civic Participation: It encourages citizens to participate in the political process. - Development of Political Culture: It helps in the development of a democratic political culture. - Promotion of Political Stability: It promotes political stability by inculcating in citizens the values of tolerance and compromise. - Facilitation of Political Change: It facilitates peaceful political change by preparing citizens to accept new political ideas and leaders.

waec-government-theory-0369.explanation: It is important for a state to have an efficient local government system for several reasons. These include: - Grassroots Development: Local governments are closer to the people and can therefore address their specific needs. - Promotion of Democracy: Local governments provide a training ground for democracy as they involve people in decision-making. - Efficient Service Delivery: Local governments can deliver services more efficiently due to their proximity to the people. - Conflict Resolution: Local governments can help resolve local disputes and maintain peace. - Economic Development: Local governments can stimulate economic development by implementing local economic policies.

waec-government-theory-0370.explanation: The study of nationalism and nationalist activities is important to the democratic development of a state for several reasons. Firstly, it fosters a sense of unity and common identity among the citizens of a state. This unity is crucial for the smooth functioning of a democratic system as it promotes cooperation and mutual understanding among the diverse groups within the state. Secondly, nationalism encourages active participation in the democratic process. When citizens feel a strong sense of belonging to their nation, they are more likely to take part in elections, voice their opinions, and engage in other democratic activities. Thirdly, nationalism can serve as a bulwark against external threats and influences. A strong sense of national identity can help to protect the democratic institutions of a state from foreign interference. Fourthly, nationalism can promote social cohesion and stability, which are essential for the effective functioning of a democratic system. Lastly, the study of nationalism and nationalist activities can provide valuable insights into the historical, cultural, and social factors that shape the democratic development of a state.

waec-government-theory-0371.explanation: A good political leader should possess several qualities. Firstly, they should have integrity. This means they should be honest, transparent, and accountable in their actions. Secondly, they should have good communication skills. They should be able to articulate their ideas clearly and persuasively, and they should also be good listeners. Thirdly, they should have a vision. They should have a clear idea of what they want to achieve and how to go about it. Fourthly, they should have the ability to inspire and motivate others. They should be able to rally their followers and inspire them to work towards a common goal.

waec-government-theory-0372.explanation: Political leadership refers to the role of individuals or groups in influencing, guiding, and directing the political activities and affairs of a state or a political entity. It involves making decisions that affect the lives of the citizens, formulating policies, implementing laws, and maintaining order and stability in the society. Political leaders can be elected officials, such as presidents and prime ministers, or they can be influential figures in political parties, social movements, or other political organizations. The effectiveness of a political leader is often measured by their ability to mobilize support, achieve their political objectives, and contribute to the overall well-being of the society.

waec-government-theory-0373.explanation: Diplomacy plays a crucial role in the development of Nigeria in several ways. Firstly, it helps to maintain peace and security. Through diplomatic negotiations and agreements, Nigeria can resolve conflicts with other countries and prevent the outbreak of war. Secondly, diplomacy enables Nigeria to establish and maintain economic ties with other countries. This can lead to increased trade, investment, and economic growth. Thirdly, diplomacy allows Nigeria to gain international support for its development goals. By engaging in diplomatic activities, Nigeria can persuade other countries and international organizations to provide financial aid, technical assistance, and other forms of support. Fourthly, diplomacy can enhance Nigeria's international reputation and influence. By acting as a responsible and constructive member of the international community, Nigeria can gain respect and influence on the global stage. Lastly, diplomacy can help to protect the rights and interests of Nigerians abroad. Through diplomatic channels, the Nigerian government can assist its citizens who are living, working, or traveling in other countries.

waec-government-theory-0374.explanation: Colonial administrations had several positive political impacts on West African States leading to statehood. Firstly, they introduced modern systems of governance, including the principles of rule of law and administrative efficiency. Secondly, they established infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports, which facilitated trade and communication. Thirdly, they introduced formal education, which produced a class of educated Africans who later became leaders in the struggle for independence. Fourthly, they brought about economic development, albeit uneven, through the introduction of cash crops and mining. Lastly, they inadvertently fostered a sense of nationalism among Africans. The experience of colonial rule, with all its injustices and inequalities, made Africans more aware of their common identity and their desire for freedom and self-determination.

waec-government-theory-0375.explanation: Democratic governance is a form of government where the supreme power is vested in the people and exercised by them directly or indirectly through a system of representation usually involving periodically held free elections. However, there are instances where democratic governance fails due to certain mistakes, which may give cause for the military to intervene in politics. Here are five such mistakes: - Corruption: This is one of the most common mistakes in democratic governance. When the elected officials engage in corrupt practices, it undermines the trust of the people in the government and can lead to military intervention to restore order and integrity. - Abuse of Power: When those in power use their position to serve their personal interests rather than the interests of the people, it can lead to dissatisfaction among the populace and create a vacuum that the military may feel compelled to fill. - Failure to uphold the rule of law: Democratic governance is based on the rule of law. When this is not upheld, it can lead to chaos and disorder, providing a reason for the military to step in. - Political Instability: Frequent changes in government, political infighting, or lack of clear leadership can lead to instability, which can be detrimental to the nation's progress. In such cases, the military may intervene to establish stability. - Infringement on Human Rights: When a democratic government fails to protect the rights of its citizens or engages in activities that infringe on these rights, it can lead to public outcry and potential military intervention. In conclusion, while democratic governance is the preferred form of government, certain mistakes can undermine its effectiveness and give cause for the military to intervene. However, it's important to note that military intervention in politics is generally viewed as a setback to democratic governance and is not a desirable outcome.

waec-government-theory-0376.explanation: Five Ways the Media Can Play a Vital Role in Making Democratic Government Work in Nigeria The media is often referred to as the "fourth estate of the realm" because of its critical role in promoting democracy. In Nigeria, where democracy is still evolving, the media ensures accountability, transparency and citizen participation in governance. Here are five key ways the media contributes to making democratic government work in Nigeria: 1. Promoting Transparency and Accountability The media serves as a watchdog, exposing corruption, mismanagement, and abuse of power by government officials. Investigative journalism helps to hold public officeholders accountable, ensuring that government actions align with the public interest. For example, media coverage of financial scandals and electoral malpractice pressures leaders to act responsibly. 2. Educating and Informing Citizens A well-informed electorate is essential for a functioning democracy. The media provides accurate and up-to-date information about government policies, political developments, and civic responsibilities. By explaining complex policies in simple terms, the media helps citizens make informed decisions, especially during elections. 3. Providing a Platform for Public Debate and Participation The media creates avenues for public discourse, where citizens can express their views on governance, social issues, and policy decisions. Platforms like radio talk shows, TV discussions, social media, and newspapers enable Nigerians to engage in meaningful conversations about national issues, strengthening democratic participation. 4. Acting as a Bridge Between the Government and the People The media plays a vital role in communicating government policies to the people and relaying public opinions to the government. Through interviews, press conferences, and policy analysis, the media ensures that both government officials and citizens understand each other's concerns, fostering a responsive and people-oriented government. 5. Monitoring Elections and Democratic Processes A democratic government relies on free, fair, and credible elections. The media plays a crucial role in covering election campaigns, reporting election irregularities, and providing real-time updates on voting processes. By acting as an independent observer, the media helps to prevent electoral fraud and strengthens public confidence in the democratic process.

waec-government-theory-0377.explanation: Five Reasons Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) Are Major Stakeholders in Nigeria’s Governance Structure Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) help to promote democracy, good governance and national development in Nigeria. As independent, non-governmental entities, they help to bridge the gap between the government and the people. Here are five key reasons why CSOs are considered major stakeholders in Nigeria’s governance structure: 1. Promoting Transparency and Accountability CSOs serve as watchdogs, monitoring government actions and policies to ensure transparency and accountability. They expose corruption, demand good governance, and push for reforms that promote efficiency and fairness in public administration. For example, organisations like the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) have consistently challenged cases of financial mismanagement in Nigeria. 2. Advocating for Human Rights and Social Justice CSOs play a critical role in protecting human rights and social justice by defending the rights of marginalized groups, women, children, and persons with disabilities. They challenge human rights violations, campaign for legal reforms, and offer support to victims of injustice. Groups like Amnesty International Nigeria and the CLEEN Foundation advocate for police reforms and justice for victims of abuse. 3. Enhancing Citizen Participation in Governance CSOs empower citizens to engage in governance by educating them on their rights, responsibilities, and civic duties. They organize town hall meetings, voter education campaigns, and public debates to ensure citizens participate actively in decision-making processes. This strengthens democracy and ensures that government policies reflect the people's interests. 4. Providing Alternative Policy Ideas and Solutions CSOs conduct research, propose policies, and engage in advocacy to improve governance and national development. They provide independent, well-researched alternatives to government policies, helping policymakers make informed decisions. Think tanks like the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD) and BudgIT Nigeria analyse government budgets and policies, offering solutions to improve economic and social governance. 5. Supporting Social and Economic Development Many CSOs focus on community development by providing healthcare, education, poverty alleviation programs, and humanitarian aid. They complement government efforts in sectors where public services are insufficient or inefficient. Organisations like ActionAid Nigeria and the Red Cross Society of Nigeria provide relief aid, empower women, and support rural development.

waec-government-theory-0378.explanation: Five Factors Behind Attacks on the Democratic System in Some ECOWAS Member States In recent years, democracy in some Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) member states has come under serious attack, leading to military coups, political instability and authoritarian rule. Several factors contribute to these challenges. Below are five key reasons: 1. Weak Democratic Institutions Many ECOWAS states struggle with fragile democratic institutions, such as weak judicial systems, compromised electoral commissions, and ineffective parliaments. These institutions often fail to uphold democratic principles, allowing election rigging, judicial manipulation, and constitutional amendments that favour incumbents. When institutions fail to function effectively, it creates a breeding ground for political instability and unconstitutional power grabs. 2. Corruption and Poor Governance Widespread corruption and mismanagement of resources weaken public trust in democratic governments. When leaders embezzle public funds, fail to provide basic services, and enrich themselves at the expense of citizens, the frustration often leads to civil unrest. In some cases, military interventions or violent protests emerge as a response to corrupt civilian rule, as seen in Guinea and Mali. 3. Electoral Fraud and Manipulation Many ECOWAS states experience elections that lack credibility, with widespread allegations of voter suppression, ballot box stuffing, and post-election violence. When political leaders refuse to accept defeat, manipulate constitutions to extend their tenure, or silence opposition parties, democracy is weakened. The loss of faith in the electoral process has led to military takeovers in countries like Niger and Burkina Faso. 4. Rising Insecurity and Terrorism West Africa faces significant security threats from terrorist groups, armed insurgencies, and banditry. When democratic governments fail to address security challenges, people begin to see the military as a better alternative for restoring order. In countries like Mali and Burkina Faso, repeated terrorist attacks and government inaction led to public support for military interventions, undermining democratic governance. 5. Foreign Influence and Geopolitical Interests External actors, including foreign powers and regional blocs, play a role in shaping political events in ECOWAS states. Some former colonial powers have been accused of supporting certain regimes for economic and strategic interests, while others impose sanctions that further destabilize governments. Additionally, military regimes sometimes receive support from neighbouring juntas, making democratic restoration difficult.

waec-government-theory-0379.explanation: (a) Three Ways the Judicial Arm of Government Sustains Democracy Upholding the Rule of Law: The judiciary ensures that all individuals, including government officials, adhere to the constitution and legal frameworks. By interpreting and enforcing laws fairly, courts prevent abuses of power and protect citizens' rights. Protecting Fundamental Human Rights: A strong judiciary safeguards freedom of speech, association, and the press, ensuring that democracy thrives. Courts hold governments accountable when they attempt to suppress civil liberties. Resolving Electoral Disputes: Courts play a key role in resolving election-related conflicts, ensuring that electoral processes remain free, fair, and credible. By adjudicating disputes fairly, they prevent political instability and maintain public confidence in democratic institutions. (b) Three Ways the Executive Arm of Government Sustains Democracy Ensuring Good Governance and Accountability: A democratic executive promotes transparency, accountability, and efficiency in governance. By implementing policies that reflect the will of the people, the executive fosters trust in democratic processes. Respecting the Principle of Separation of Powers: The executive should function within its constitutional limits and avoid interfering with the judiciary or legislature. This allows checks and balances to operate effectively, preventing dictatorship or authoritarianism. Protecting National Security and Stability: The executive is responsible for maintaining law and order while respecting human rights. By effectively tackling security challenges like terrorism, insurgency, and electoral violence, the executive ensures a peaceful environment for democracy to flourish.

waec-government-theory-0380.explanation: Five Reasons Why Peace Education is Vital in a State Like Nigeria Prevention of Political and Ethnic Conflicts: Nigeria has experienced major political crises, often fuelled by ethnic and religious differences. Peace education teaches tolerance, conflict resolution, and dialogue, helping to reduce tensions and prevent violent clashes. Promotion of National Unity and Cohesion: Peace education fosters a sense of shared identity among citizens by emphasizing values such as cooperation, respect for diversity, and patriotism. This is essential in a multi-ethnic country like Nigeria, where divisions often threaten national stability. Reduction of Electoral Violence and Political Instability: Many political crises in Nigeria stem from election-related violence and disputes. Peace education helps citizens understand the importance of democratic principles, non-violent political participation, and respect for electoral outcomes, thereby reducing electoral conflicts. Encouragement of Rule of Law and Human Rights Protection: When people are educated on peaceful coexistence, they are more likely to respect laws, democratic institutions, and human rights. This leads to a more stable society where disputes are resolved through legal means rather than violence. Enhancement of Sustainable Development: A peaceful society creates an enabling environment for economic growth, education, and social progress. Investors, businesses, and international organizations are more likely to engage with a nation that is stable, ensuring long-term development.

waec-government-theory-0381.explanation: Five Debilitating Effects of French Colonial Rule in French West African Colonies Suppression of Indigenous Political Systems: The French policy of Assimilation undermined traditional African governance structures, replacing them with French administrative systems. This disrupted indigenous leadership and weakened the ability of local rulers to govern effectively. Exploitation of Economic Resources: The French extracted raw materials like gold, cocoa, and cotton for the benefit of France, leaving the colonies economically dependent and underdeveloped. Infrastructure was built mainly to facilitate resource extraction, not local economic growth. Limited Educational and Social Development: Unlike British colonies that allowed some level of self-rule, the French strictly controlled education, producing a small elite class loyal to France while keeping the majority of the population illiterate and unskilled. This created a long-term developmental gap. Forced Labour and Heavy Taxation: The French imposed harsh forced labour policies (such as the corvée system), where Africans were required to work on colonial projects without pay. High taxation further worsened economic hardship, leading to widespread poverty and resentment. Fragmentation and Weak National Identity: The artificial boundaries drawn by the French disregarded ethnic and cultural identities, leading to divided societies with weak national consciousness. The continued influence of Francophone policies after independence further hindered regional integration.

waec-government-theory-0382.explanation: Five Ways ECOWAS Can Operate to Achieve Its Stated Objectives The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was established in 1975 to promote economic integration and political stability among its 15 member states. To achieve its objectives effectively, ECOWAS can operate in the following ways: Enhancing Economic Integration and Free Trade: ECOWAS can fully implement the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS) to ensure free movement of goods and services across member states. This will boost intra-regional trade, reduce reliance on external markets, and strengthen West Africa’s economic stability. Strengthening Regional Security and Conflict Resolution: The ECOWAS Standby Force and Mediation Mechanisms should be actively deployed to resolve political crises, military coups, and insurgencies within the region. By strengthening the ECOWAS Early Warning System, the organization can proactively prevent conflicts before they escalate. Improving Infrastructure and Regional Connectivity: ECOWAS can expand transnational road networks, railway systems, and energy projects to improve connectivity among member states. This will facilitate faster movement of people and goods, enhance economic development, and attract foreign investment. Promoting Democratic Governance and Human Rights: ECOWAS can enforce its Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance by ensuring free and fair elections, discouraging unconstitutional changes of government, and holding leaders accountable. This will foster political stability and stronger institutions in member states. Facilitating Free Movement of Citizens and Labour Mobility: ECOWAS can enhance its free movement policy by eliminating travel restrictions, border delays, and bureaucratic bottlenecks that hinder West Africans from working and residing in other member states. A more integrated labour market will help in job creation and economic empowerment.
